questions.stem: The remainder when 250 is divided by 12, written $250\bmod 12$, is
questions.explanation: Since $12\times20=240$ and $250-240=10$, the remainder is $10$. In congruence form $250\equiv10\pmod{12}$. The remainder must always be smaller than the divisor $12$, which rules out $20$.

optionRationale.1: This subtracts from the multiple above, $252-250$, instead of measuring from the multiple below $250$.
optionRationale.2: $20$ is the quotient, not the remainder.
optionRationale.4: This is the remainder on dividing $250$ by $6$, not by $12$.

questions.objective: Find the remainder in modular arithmetic

questions.stem: A can finish a piece of work in 15 days and B can finish the same work in 10 days. Working together, they will finish it in
questions.explanation: A does $\tfrac1{15}$ of the work per day and B does $\tfrac1{10}$. Together they do $\tfrac1{15}+\tfrac1{10}=\tfrac{2+3}{30}=\tfrac16$ per day, so the whole work takes $6$ days.

optionRationale.2: This takes the plain average of $15$ and $10$, which is not how work rates combine.
optionRationale.3: This adds the numbers of days instead of adding the daily rates.
optionRationale.4: This is half of the faster worker's time, which would hold only if both workers were equally fast.

questions.objective: Combine work rates of two workers

questions.stem: The smallest positive integer $x$ satisfying the congruence $7x\equiv3\pmod{11}$ is
questions.explanation: Test small values: $7\cdot1=7$, $7\cdot2=14=11+3$, so $7\cdot2\equiv3\pmod{11}$. Alternatively the inverse of $7$ modulo $11$ is $8$ because $56\equiv1$, giving $x\equiv8\cdot3=24\equiv2$. So $x=2$.

optionRationale.2: $7\cdot8=56\equiv1\pmod{11}$; $8$ is the inverse of $7$, not the solution.

questions.stem: A 40-litre mixture of milk and water has milk and water in the ratio $3:1$. How much water must be added so that the ratio of milk to water becomes $3:2$?
questions.explanation: In 40 L at ratio $3:1$ there are $30$ L of milk and $10$ L of water. For a ratio $3:2$ with $30$ L of milk, water must be $20$ L. So $20-10=10$ L of water must be added.

optionRationale.1: This takes half of the water already present instead of solving $30:x=3:2$.
optionRationale.3: $20$ L is the total water needed afterwards; the $10$ L already present must be subtracted.
optionRationale.4: $30$ L is the quantity of milk, not the amount of water to be added.

questions.objective: Adjust a mixture ratio by adding one component

questions.stem: A can complete a job in 20 days and B in 30 days. A starts alone and works for 5 days, and then B joins him and they finish the job together. The number of days for which they work together is
questions.explanation: In 5 days A completes $\tfrac5{20}=\tfrac14$ of the job, leaving $\tfrac34$. Together they do $\tfrac1{20}+\tfrac1{30}=\tfrac1{12}$ per day, so the remaining work takes $\tfrac34\times12=9$ days.

optionRationale.2: $12$ days is the time the two would need for the whole job together, ignoring A's first 5 days.
optionRationale.3: This is the time for A alone to do the remaining $\tfrac34$ of the job at $\tfrac1{20}$ per day, ignoring B.
optionRationale.4: This halves the remaining time incorrectly, as if B were as fast as A.

questions.objective: Solve a work problem with a delayed start

questions.stem: The integers $x$ satisfying both $3x+2>11$ and $2x-1\le9$ are collected together. Their sum is
questions.explanation: From $3x+2>11$ we get $x>3$. From $2x-1\le9$ we get $x\le5$. So the integers are $4$ and $5$, and their sum is $9$.

optionRationale.2: This includes $x=3$ by treating the strict inequality $x>3$ as $x\ge3$, giving $3+4+5$.
optionRationale.3: $5$ is only the largest solution, not the sum of all the solutions.
optionRationale.4: This also includes $x=6$, which fails $2x-1\le9$ because $11>9$.

questions.objective: Combine linear inequalities in one variable

questions.stem: A boat takes 3 hours to go 15 km upstream and 2 hours to go 20 km downstream in a river. The time it takes to cover 30 km downstream and then return 30 km upstream is
questions.explanation: Upstream speed is $15/3=5$ km/h and downstream speed is $20/2=10$ km/h. Hence the 30 km downstream trip takes $3$ h and the 30 km upstream trip takes $6$ h, a total of $9$ hours.

optionRationale.1: This uses the still-water speed $7.5$ km/h for both legs, giving $4+4$ hours.
optionRationale.2: This uses the still-water speed for the downstream leg only, giving $4+6$ hours.
optionRationale.4: This uses the upstream speed for both legs, $30/5+30/5=12$ hours, ignoring the help from the stream.

questions.objective: Compute round-trip time from upstream and downstream speeds

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): In a 100 m race, if A beats B by 10 m, then the ratio of the speeds of A and B is $10:9$.
Reason (R): In the time A runs 100 m, B runs only 90 m.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: A beats B by 10 m means that when A has covered 100 m, B has covered 90 m in the same time. Since speed is proportional to distance in equal time, the speeds are in the ratio $100:90=10:9$. So both statements are true and the reason gives the assertion.

optionRationale.2: The reason is not just true, it is exactly the basis of the ratio, so it explains the assertion.
optionRationale.3: The reason is true, since B has covered only 90 m at the moment A finishes.
optionRationale.4: The assertion is true: $100:90$ simplifies to $10:9$.

questions.objective: Relate a winning margin in a race to the ratio of speeds

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about congruence modulo $n$.
A. If $a\equiv b$ and $c\equiv d\pmod n$ then $a+c\equiv b+d\pmod n$.
B. If $a\equiv b$ and $c\equiv d\pmod n$ then $ac\equiv bd\pmod n$.
C. If $ac\equiv bc\pmod n$ then $a\equiv b\pmod n$ always.
D. If $a\equiv b\pmod n$ then $a^2\equiv b^2\pmod n$.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Congruences can be added, multiplied and raised to powers, so A, B and D hold. C fails when $c$ and $n$ share a factor: $2\cdot3=6\equiv0=2\cdot0\pmod 6$, yet $3\not\equiv0\pmod 6$. Cancelling is allowed only when $c$ is coprime to $n$.

optionRationale.1: C is false in general, so including it makes this option wrong.
optionRationale.2: C is false, and this option also leaves out the true statement D.
optionRationale.4: C is false, and this option also drops B and D, which are both true.

questions.objective: Recall the rules of operating with congruences
